Gold erases gains as Nvidia optimism fades and US moves to restore tariffs to 2025 levels
body: Gold erased all the weekly gains yesterday as the market optimism from Nvidia news faded rather quickly. The catalyst seemed to be the WSJ report saying that the US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and other countries as early as this week.

After the Supreme Court ruling, the Trump administration has been attempting to recreate a similar tariff structure through a different legal route, with country-specific investigations providing the justification.

This basically means that the Supreme Court ruling might have temporarily disrupted the tariff agenda without producing a lasting reduction in the effective tariff burden. So, we are going back to broadly similar levels to those imposed in 2025.

According to the Financial Times, the US is expected to honour previous trade agreements by capping the new tariffs for countries that had negotiated deals with the Trump administration. Overall, this isn’t a major gamechanger, but it still adds to inflation and growth concerns.

For gold, it’s a tricky situation because it keeps getting smashed lower when the stock market falls on growth concerns and the gains are capped when the sentiment improves because the US dollar and real yields get support from the hawkish repricing.

Looking ahead, gold will likely need support from a dovish repricing in interest rate expectations either from weaker data, dovish Fed commentary or an end to the Iran war. But buyers will also need to be aware that a dovish repricing from renewed stock market selloff could lead to more liquidations.

On the daily chart, we can see that gold (CFD contract) erased the recent gains and it’s now approaching the key 3,500 level again. We can expect the buyers to step in around the 3,500 level, with a defined risk below it, to position for a rally into the downward trendline. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to target the 3,100 level next.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. We can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into the major downward trendline next.

On the 1 hour chart, the support zone around the 3,600 level turned into resistance now. If we get a bounce from the 3,500 level, we can expect the sellers to step in around the resistance and the trendline, with a defined risk above the trendline, to position for a drop into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into the major downward trendline next. The red lines define the average daily range for today.
Today we have the US Core PCE price index and the latest US Jobless Claims figures.

news.title: Gold is losing its grip again as sellers eye a break of the $3,500 level
body: After an early bounce on Monday, gold stumbled in trading yesterday and is down another 1% today and we're already staring at another test of the $3,500 mark. The precious metal is on course for a third straight weekly decline and its sixth in seven weeks. Ouch.
As much as the selling pressures might seem excessive, the fact of the matter is that not much has changed from a technical standpoint this week.

The break below the 100-week moving average (red line) just under $4,000 remains the elephant in the room. That was the first serious breach of the key technical level since 2023 and has disrupted the upside momentum in gold that has helped to sustain the stunning rally for much of the last two years.

As seen with the chart above, what looks to be alarming is that if $3,500 gives way, there isn't much in the way of any major technical support until the $3,000-$3,140 region. That's where the 200-week moving average (blue line) and the 61.8 Fib retracement level of the broader rally come into play. That suggests there is quite a bit of air underneath the current price level.

And as mentioned yesterday, I still like the long-term story for gold. However, there's a difference between liking the asset proposition and liking the trade that is right in front of you. Even if gold is at the cheapest levels for this year, it doesn't mean that it is time to go bargain hunting just yet.

In essence, dip buyers have to prove that they have staying power above $3,500 for an extended period to even be taken seriously at this point. Otherwise, it feels like it is only a matter of time before the next wave of selling hits and we go in search of the next ledge for gold to try and hang on to.

news.title: UBS sees gold at $5,000 by end-2027, well above Goldman's $4,650 call
body: A $5,000 target from a major wealth manager strengthens the long-term bull case for gold, but UBS's own list of headwinds is a reminder that the near-term path runs through the Fed. With US policy on a hiking path and the dollar firm, gold remains sensitive to every shift in rate expectations, including Wednesday's PCE inflation data. Any sign that Fed tightening is nearing its end would likely be the trigger for gold to start closing the gap toward bank forecasts. Steady central bank buying offers a floor of demand, which helps explain why forecasters remain confident on the 2027 outlook despite this year's weakness.
UBS is sticking with gold, forecasting $5,000 an ounce by end-2027 on central bank demand and debt worries, even as higher US real yields and a strong dollar keep the metal under pressure for now.

UBS Global Wealth Management has reaffirmed its constructive view on gold, keeping the metal rated Attractive and forecasting that it will reach $5,000 an ounce by December 2027. The call, set out in a note on portfolio positioning after a volatile stretch for markets, implies a gain of more than a third from the level of around $3,600 referenced in the note, and places UBS toward the top of the major banks' forecasts.

The bank sees gold's role as strategic rather than tactical. It points to four lasting supports: continued diversification of central bank reserves away from traditional holdings, high and rising sovereign debt, persistent geopolitical uncertainty, and demand from China. Together, UBS argues, these give the metal a place in portfolios as a source of return that does not depend on the same drivers as stocks and bonds.

UBS is also clear about what has been holding gold back. Higher US real yields, a strong dollar and liquidity-driven selling have all weighed on prices, and those pressures have been sharpened by the Federal Reserve's return to rate increases this year. Gold has struggled through much of 2026 as markets priced a higher path for US interest rates, and its moves have often tracked rate expectations more closely than geopolitical headlines.

The UBS target stands out against recent calls from other banks. Goldman Sachs expects gold to climb back above $4,600 and reach $4,650 by the end of 2027, arguing that structural central bank buying will eventually win out even as higher rate expectations slow the metal in the near term. CIBC cut its forecast for the current quarter to $4,500 last month but sees a rebound to $5,200 in 2027. The common thread is that central bank demand underpins the long-term case, while the timing depends heavily on the Fed.

For UBS, gold sits alongside a broader push for diversification. The bank argues that in a world where government policy increasingly drives economic outcomes and market leadership is concentrated in a small number of large technology companies, investors should spread their sources of return more widely. It also sees a role for diversified commodity exposure, including copper, to help portfolios cope with inflation, geopolitical shocks, climate disruption and supply risks.

The path to $5,000 is likely to depend on when US rate expectations peak. A pause in Fed tightening, or a turn lower in real yields and the dollar, would remove the main obstacles UBS has identified, while continued central bank purchases provide a steady source of demand in the meantime.

news.title: Four ways to own gold, and the new one JPMorgan and HSBC just tested in London
body: The pilot changes how gold is held and moved, not how much investors want, so it has little bearing on prices near term. Spot gold remains under pressure from near-certain expectations of a December Fed hike and sits not far above last week's more-than-one-year low. The longer-term effect could be supportive. Gold that can be pledged as collateral in real time earns a role on institutional balance sheets beyond being a store of value. For crypto, the pilot adds institutional competition to on-chain gold tokens such as XAUT and PAXG. It also gives regulators a working wholesale model to point to as the FCA shapes its rules for tokenised gold.
Gold has always been trusted and hard to move; London's biggest dealers have now tested a way to keep the trust and lose some of the weight.

JPMorgan, HSBC and StoneX have completed the first live, legally binding trades in a new form of gold ownership in London, the World Gold Council said on November 24. The three firms traded and settled fractional ownership interests in physical gold bars, and used those interests as collateral, without moving any metal out of the vault.

The structure is called a Pooled Gold Interest (PGI), and it is still at pilot stage. But it targets one of the oldest frictions in the bullion market: gold is valuable, trusted and heavy, and the last of those makes it awkward to use. To see why the PGI matters, it helps to understand the three main ways gold is already held, and where the new option sits between them.

The London market runs on 400-ounce Good Delivery bars. London vaults held about 9,850 tonnes of gold at the end of October, according to LBMA monthly data. The World Gold Council puts over-the-counter trading in the city at more than $180 billion a day.

Almost none of that trading involves bars changing hands. Moving a bar means insuring it, transporting it and recording it, and a single bar is worth around $1.4 million at current prices. So most of the market trades claims on gold rather than gold itself. Each ownership model answers the same two questions differently: what exactly do you own, and what happens if the institution holding it fails?
What you own: specific, numbered bars, held in your name and kept separate from the custodian's own assets.
The trade-off: this is the safest form of ownership, because the bars are yours if the custodian goes bust. But bars can't be split, and transferring ownership is slow and costly.
What you own: a claim on a bullion bank for a quantity of gold, backed by the bank's general pool of metal.

The trade-off: unallocated accounts carry most of London's trading because they're flexible. Any amount can be traded and settled without touching a bar. The catch is that the holder is a creditor of the bank, not the owner of any metal. If the bank fails, the holder joins the queue.
What you own: a proprietary interest in a pool of segregated physical bars, transferred electronically.

The trade-off: the PGI tries to combine the strengths of the first two models. Like allocated gold, it is ownership rather than a claim on a bank. Like unallocated gold, it can be split into fractions and moved quickly. In the pilot, bars were placed into the system, interests were created, traded and settled, and the gold was then withdrawn to complete the cycle. Mark Amlin, JPMorgan's global head of physical commodities, said gold ownership that is fractional, readily transferable and "insolvency remote" would let gold be used more widely, including as collateral.

ICE Benchmark Administration operates the system and Baton Systems provides the settlement technology. Notably, the World Gold Council's announcement describes a real-time settlement layer and does not say the system runs on a blockchain.
What you own: a crypto token, such as Tether Gold (XAUT) or Paxos's PAX Gold (PAXG), each representing one troy ounce of physical gold held by the issuer.

news.title: Goldman sees TOPIX up 20% to 4,500 and names five themes for Japanese stocks in 2027
body: Goldman's call hinges on continued global AI spending, which leaves Japanese stocks exposed to the same AI-funding doubts that have hit US technology shares this month. The expected broadening could favour mid-cap restructuring candidates, trading houses, shippers and energy firms over the crowded AI and bank trades that led this year. A steady flow of takeover bids and buyouts would add a deal premium across the market. On the macro side, further Bank of Japan hikes, made more likely by Wednesday's hot services inflation reading, would lift the yen and could weigh on exporters. It would, however, support the banks' earnings base.

Goldman Sachs expects another strong year for Japanese stocks, with the TOPIX seen at 4,500, but says the rally should rely less on AI and banks and more on restructuring, robotics, energy security and a government push for companies to spend.

Japanese stocks are set to rally again over the coming year, but the drivers of the gains are likely to change, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The bank's strategists project the TOPIX index will rise about 20% to 4,500 over the next 12 months, based on forecasts for earnings per share growth of 9% in fiscal 2027, as long as global spending on artificial intelligence continues.

Bruce Kirk, Goldman's chief Japan equity strategist, describes 2027 as a transitional year for the market. Gains over the past three years have been driven mainly by AI-related stocks, banks and the Bank of Japan's move away from ultra-loose policy. Kirk expects the rally to broaden as investors diversify into less crowded and less volatile themes, and as the government steps up efforts to get companies to put their cash to work.

That policy push is coordinated across Tokyo. Kirk points to a consistent message from the Tokyo Stock Exchange, the Financial Services Agency, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration, all encouraging firms to use excess cash reserves to fund future growth. Japan's revised corporate governance code now emphasises growth-oriented governance and fair treatment of minority shareholders in mergers.

Goldman argues that lifting the TOPIX's return on equity, which still lags many global markets, will require more forceful restructuring than has occurred so far, including mergers, segment overhauls and sector consolidation. It expects a significant rise in takeover bids, management buyouts and industry consolidation from 2027.

Kirk identifies five themes for investors. The first is AI innovation and quality, with higher-quality AI-related companies having outperformed their peers. The second is corporate restructuring. The third is physical AI: labour costs for non-financial TOPIX companies rose to 10.5% of sales in fiscal 2025, a decade high, while Goldman expects humanoid robot prices to halve to about $21,000 by 2035, and the government is targeting 350,000 AI robots by 2030. The fourth is energy and resource security. Japan imports almost all of its oil, gas, coal and critical minerals, and its energy self-sufficiency, at 16% in 2024, remains low. Government plans to diversify supply and expand solar, thermal and advanced nuclear power could benefit trading houses, shipping firms, energy companies and heavy industry, with overlap seen with projects under the $550 billion US-Japan trade deal. The fifth is cybersecurity, where Tokyo wants domestic firms to reach annual revenue of more than 3 trillion yen by 2035.

The energy theme is already playing out. Japan this week agreed to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to refill its strategic reserve, while giving Riyadh more storage capacity on Japanese soil.
